Theories.  The  most  systematic  explana 
tions  arc  those  of  Lipps  and  Wuudt.  (i) 
Lipps  sets  up  a  principle:  of  mechanical- 
aesthetic  unity,  in  virtue  of  which  every 
space  form  is  endowed  by  us,  in  idea,  with  a 
living  personality,  or  regarded  as  the  scene 
of  the  interplay  of  mechanical  forces.  Our 
judgments  of  comparison  are  modified,  uncon 
sciously,  by  this  anthropomorphic  attitude. 
The  circle,  for  example,  is  the  result  of  the 
action  of  tangential  and  radial  forces,  in  which 
the  radial  seems  to  triumph  ;  the  figure  has 
therefore  a  centripetal  character,  which  leads 
to  underestimation:  Fig.  13  looks  smaller 
than  14,  though  the  height  and  breadth  of 
both  is  the  same.  (2)  "Wumlt  makes  the
